title: Failover drill: dispatch database
scratchpad:
DRILL in staging, not an incident
replica promotion 90s (target < 2 min)
workers cached old address ~4 min -> Teodor: 30s by Oct 15
paging -> rotation (Jun), runbook rewrite (Odette)
prod drill: no date yet
segments: This is the debrief for this morning's failover drill. To be clear for anyone reading these notes later, nothing broke for customers. This was staging, on purpose.
Right. It's a game day, not an incident. We picked the dispatch database because it's the one thing the scheduler can't live without.
The plan was simple. Stop the primary database in staging, let the replica take over, and watch whether the scheduler keeps assigning jobs.
We ran a synthetic workload against it, roughly a normal Tuesday's worth of bookings squeezed into an hour.
The replica promotion itself was fine. It took ninety seconds from the moment the primary stopped to the replica accepting writes.
Our target was under two minutes, so yes. The database did its job.
The problem was everything around it. The scheduler workers kept trying the old primary for about four minutes, because they'd cached the database address.
So the database was back in ninety seconds, and our own code ignored it for another four minutes. That's the part that would hurt in production.
The address is cached for five minutes. Nobody remembers why. I think it was a default that nobody ever changed.
What would a technician see during those four minutes?
New bookings queue up. Nothing's lost, but dispatchers would see jobs stuck as pending, and they'd start phoning people to ask what's going on.
The second finding is alerting. The page went out, but to the wrong person.
The alert was still routed to my old phone number from before the rotation existed. The rotation is in the team calendar, but the paging tool never got told.
That one's embarrassing, but it's easy. The paging tool should read the same schedule as the calendar.
Third, the runbook. We had one, but it describes the setup from two years ago. Two of the commands in it don't even exist anymore.
So the database is fine, and our caching, paging and docs aren't. What do we change?
For the address caching, I'll drop it from five minutes to thirty seconds and make the workers retry the new primary straight away. I can have that in by the fifteenth of October.
Thirty seconds is fine for the database lookups. It's a tiny amount of extra traffic.
I'll rewrite the failover runbook from scratch, using what we actually did today, step by step. I'll walk the team through it once it's done.
And I'll connect the paging tool to the rotation, so whoever is on call that week gets paged, not whoever happened to set up the alert.
When do we do this for real, in production?
Not until the runbook is rewritten and the caching fix is live. I'd rather not pick a date today and then have to move it.
Fair. We'll pick a date once those two are done. Same scope, the dispatch database, during a quiet hour.
Should we also drill the job queue itself? That's the other single point of failure.
Eventually. One thing at a time. The database first, then the queue.
Can we write down what good looks like, so next time we can call it a pass or a fail?
Yes. The bar for the production drill: the scheduler is assigning jobs again within two minutes of the primary stopping, and the right person gets paged.
Two minutes end to end, not just the database. I like that much better.
Good. Thanks, all. This was a useful morning, even if staging took a beating.

items.text: Failover drill in staging: replica promotion took 90 seconds (target under two minutes); scheduler workers kept using the old primary for about four minutes
Cut database address caching from five minutes to thirty seconds and retry the new primary immediately, by October 15
Rewrite the failover runbook from today's drill
Connect the paging tool to the on-call rotation
Production drill pass bar: scheduler assigning jobs within two minutes of the primary stopping, and the right person paged; no date until the runbook and caching fix are done
